source.title: Removable and/or Repeated Units Emerge in Overparametrized Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Stephen Casper; X. Boix; Vanessa D'Amario; Ling Guo; Martin Schrimpf; Kasper Vinken; Gabriel Kreiman

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present. Some figure values are not recoverable from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether increasing network width preserves or improves test accuracy, using several architectures and datasets rather than the one-hidden-layer ReLU networks in V2.
record.gate_note: The paper measures test accuracy across model widths (Fig. 1) and measures prunability and redundancy across widths. It reports random-label training accuracy, but does not report held-out accuracy for the random-label models. Interpretability measurements are outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own width-versus-held-out-accuracy results in convolutional architectures, bearing on V2 in new settings. It also reports random-label fitting and plots random-label test accuracy, bearing on V1, and compares coupled batch-size/learning-rate changes, bearing on V5's adapted-recipe clause.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors propose that wider networks develop greater proportions of prunable and/or redundant units alongside maintained or improved generalization. They treat these as effective-complexity constraints, while acknowledging that their emergence alone does not imply generalization and leaving causal explanations to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper scales widths in established architectures and measures test accuracy plus unit prunability and redundancy; it does not use V2's one-hidden-layer ReLU setup or identify interpolation.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured balance of prunability and redundancy varies with initialization, dataset, architecture, and optimizer. Batch size, learning rate, and training time past convergence had no discernible effect on the reported prunability and redundancy trends in the tested cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Prunable and redundant units generally increase faster than network width, including in models fitting random labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width can increase unit-level compressibility disproportionately, but this property alone does not establish generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimizer choice changes redundancy in MLPs trained on synthetic 10,000-dimensional teacher-labeled inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimization affects activation redundancy in synthetic-data MLPs.

record.problems: Figure 1's accuracy values are not recoverable from the supplied text. ImageNet prunability points are single trials; error bars for redundancy reflect sampling variation. Random-label results report training fit and frivolous-unit measures, not held-out performance.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. The plotted accuracy values were retained as figure-only rows because the text describes the trend but the exact values cannot be recovered.

untested.parts: The exact unregularized matched-recipe comparison in V1 is not established. Random-label held-out accuracy is plotted, but chance-level performance cannot be verified from the supplied text.

Zero-training-error thresholds, continued improvement specifically beyond those thresholds, and training to convergence without explicit regularization in the original one-hidden-layer image-classification setting are not established.
The optimizer comparison uses synthetic teacher-labeled data rather than the image or language benchmarks named by V4; readable held-out optimizer differences are unavailable.
No isolated increase in batch size with learning rate held unchanged, no established workload-dependent threshold, and no language-model experiment.
Regularizer comparisons report prunability and redundancy rather than dropout's effect on held-out error.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or ranking of generalization-gap measures.
No removal of memorized training examples and retraining comparison.

missing.what: Separate random-label training-fit rows: AlexNet and ResNet56 at widths of 1x or greater achieve at least 99% training accuracy.

Separate natural- and random-label test-accuracy rows from Figure 1b. Random-label held-out accuracy is plotted, contrary to the record's assertion; its numerical level cannot be recovered from this text.
Separate unregularized AlexNet width comparisons under Gaussian and uniform Glorot, He, and LeCun initializations.

Held-out accuracy across widths under coupled batch-size/learning-rate changes. Captions explicitly report stable accuracy trends; retain fixed-epoch ResNet18 and ResNet56 separately from early-stopped AlexNet.
missing.locator: Figures E10a–E11a; Appendix D training schedules

record.verdict_notes: No full V1 verdict is justified because the supplied figure text does not establish chance-level random-label test accuracy. Missing numerical coordinates do not erase explicitly stated qualitative accuracy trends. The supplied paper is the 2021 version; the record's AAAI 2019 attribution is incorrect.

versions.untested_parts: The paper cites Zhang et al. on memorizing random labels, but does not test natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy under the same recipes.
The paper does not test one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10, identify the width needed for zero training error, or report a test-error peak around interpolation.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks on image generalization.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers and SGD on held-out performance.
No test of large-batch generalization gaps under fixed epoch budgets.
No test of dropout's effect on held-out error.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of generalization-gap measures.
No removal of memorized examples followed by test-accuracy measurement.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Varied network width and measured ImageNet validation top-1 accuracy.
rows.note: The authors state that increasing model size resulted in equal or improved performance; the plotted values are not recoverable from the supplied text.
rows.check: Equal or improved accuracy supports the width trend, but does not establish continuing improvement beyond zero training error. Training uses batch normalization, weight decay, and augmentation.

rows.subject: AlexNet and ResNet56
rows.operation_detail: Measured randomly ablated units' effect on the proportion of test labels left unchanged across widths.
rows.value: gmin > 2 for all but ResNet56 trained on random labels
rows.locator: Figure 4a; Section 5, “Prunability and redundancy develop in networks trained on random labels”
rows.note: The study says AlexNet and ResNet56 models of 1x size or greater fit random training labels with at least 99% accuracy; it does not report random-label test accuracy.
rows.check: Prunability measures preservation of predictions after unit ablation, not any listed claim. Split the architectures because random-label ResNet56 is the exception to the reported gain exceeding two. The accompanying random-label training accuracy belongs in a separate V1 row.

rows.subject: AlexNet and ResNet56
rows.operation_detail: Measured linearly redundant units across widths using PCA on test-set activations.
rows.locator: Figure 4a; Section 5, “Prunability and redundancy develop in networks trained on random labels”
rows.note: The authors report that random-label fitting and growth in frivolous units do not imply generalization.
rows.check: Activation redundancy does not measure any listed version. Its reported gain exceeding two can be retained as an out-of-version finding.

relationships.display_finding: Held-out accuracy stayed equal or improved across the tested widths, without establishing zero training error or improvement beyond its threshold.
